brief: A tool rack that hangs on a wall from keyhole hangers, with hooks for small hand tools.

requirements.requirement: Hangs on a wall from keyhole hangers
requirements.evidence: Two hex-acc-keyhole accessories (accessory:0#-1,0#2 and accessory:0#1,0#2) on the back faces of the two end cells. They drop onto screws already in the wall. The configurator checks fit only: it doesn't judge how much weight the hangers or screws can hold.

Six hex-acc-hook plates with two hooks each (12 hooks) on the front faces of the top-storey cells (accessory:1#...#4 and #5). For staging, the hooks show a gaffer tape roll and a cable coil, the only props the configurator hangs on hooks. No hand tool is staged on one, and fit is checked, not load.
Six full bases in a 3×2 grid (two storeys), with snaps, end caps and joint bolts. check_build: no rule errors, meshClash clear.

finish.summary: I built a wall tool rack: a row of three hex cells, two storeys tall (6 bases). Two keyhole hangers sit on the back of the bottom row, and six hook plates with two hooks each (12 hooks) are on the front of the top row. I put the hooks on the top storey because the configurator models the rack standing on the bench, and from the bottom row anything hanging would have gone through the bench. I capped the open faces and bolted the joints (house rules), which brings it to 52 parts. That's more than the usual ~40, but a 6-cell rack with those extras needs it. check_build found no rule errors and no mesh clashes. To show the hooks in use I hung a roll of gaffer tape and a coiled cable. They are the only things the configurator lets hang on a wall hook, so I couldn't stage an actual hand tool on one. A second roll of tape was refused because it would overlap the cable.

lines.label: Edge cap · male, two stories tall
M6 x 20 socket head screw, ISO 4762
M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
